paper_metadata.title: Bootstrapped Self Training for Knowledge Base Population.
paper_metadata.abstract: A central challenge in relation extraction is the lack of supervised training data. Pattern-based relation extractors suffer from low recall, whereas distant supervision yields noisy data which hurts precision. We propose bootstrapped self-training to capture the benefits of both systems: the precision of patterns and the generalizability of trained models. We show that training on the output of patterns drastically improves performance over the patterns. We propose self-training for further improvement: recall can be improved by incorporating the predictions from previous iterations; precision by filtering the assumed negatives based previous predictions. We show that even our pattern-based model achieves good performance on the task, and the self-trained models rank among the top systems.

problem_addressed: The paper addresses relation extraction for knowledge-base population when manually supervised training data is scarce. It seeks to combine the high precision but low recall of hand-written patterns with the broader generalization of learned models, while controlling semantic drift and the precision loss caused by noisy or assumed-negative training examples.

methodology.description: The system starts with manually developed high-precision Tokensregex and Semgrex relation patterns, supplemented by Stanford OpenIE. Their predictions over the large unlabeled source corpus become positive training examples. A traditional L1-regularized logistic-regression extractor and a bidirectional LSTM sentence classifier are trained using these examples, supervised data, assumed negatives, and hand annotations. In subsequent self-training, predictions from the learned extractors are removed from the negative pool; for the submitted conservative version, positives remain the pattern outputs while negatives are regenerated. Six extractors—patterns, OpenIE, website, alternate names, supervised logistic regression, and neural LSTM—are optionally combined by a classifier using extractor-agreement and relation features. Predictions are stored and processed in a relational database before consistency/inference for slot filling or direct submission for the KB track.

ontology_or_schema_use.value: The extractors map OpenIE and other relation predictions into the KBP relation schema. Candidate relation mentions are type-checked using subject and object named-entity tags, and the system uses canonical entity links represented by Wikipedia titles or canonical surface forms. The paper does not describe a separately formalized ontology or schema-discovery procedure.

input_output.input_type: Unstructured textual sentences from the KBP source corpora, enriched with POS tags, lemmas, named-entity tags, dependency parses, entity mentions, and canonical entity links.
input_output.input_granularity: Relation-mention level: candidate pairs of entity mentions constrained to occur in the same sentence and to satisfy relation-compatible entity types; the broader system aggregates these predictions into hop-0 and hop-1 KBP queries and knowledge-base entries.
input_output.output_representation: Extracted typed relations associated with canonical entity pairs and provenance sentences; these relation predictions are materialized as a coherent knowledge base in a relational database, submitted directly for the KB track, or passed to a consistency and inference component for slot filling.

evaluation.setting: The system was evaluated in the 2015 KBP slot-filling and cold-start KB tracks. Slot-filling results report hop-0, hop-1, and all-hop scores for four submitted configurations in Table 1. KB-track results report the same breakdown for high-precision and high-recall configurations in Table 2. Development used propagated 2013 annotations, slower 2010–2013 end-to-end evaluation, and 2014 cold-start data for model-combination training; 2014 slot-filling data was unused.

value: Table 1 slot filling: model combination (Stanford1) achieved hop-0 P/R/F1 52.2/20.1/29.1, hop-1 26.4/4.6/7.8, and all-hop 46.8/14.4/22.0.

Table 1 slot filling: the high-precision system (Stanford2) achieved all-hop P/R/F1 51.8/10.5/17.4; the high-recall union (Stanford3) achieved 27.9/25.6/26.7; patterns only (Stanford4) achieved 54.3/10.6/17.7.
Table 2 KB track: high-precision (Stanford1) achieved hop-0 53.0/11.6/19.0, hop-1 36.7/5.0/8.8, and all-hop 48.7/9.1/15.4; high-recall (Stanford2) achieved all-hop 21.0/23.2/22.1.

The authors report that the pattern extractor alone had nearly 60% precision with recall above 10% and was unmatched by similar systems at that recall; the paper also states that the model-combination approach improved hop-0 precision by 18 F1 with only a 5 F1 recall drop in an earlier comparison.

The paper reports that high-recall systems consistently outperformed high-precision counterparts in the reported test results, suggesting a development/test mismatch and potential value from further recall-oriented self-training.

value: The method uses high-precision patterns to anchor self-training and mitigate semantic drift.
It combines pattern precision with learned-model generalizability and can exploit a very large unlabeled corpus.
The relational-database architecture makes candidate generation, corpus analytics, debugging, aggregation, and evaluation queries more direct and scalable.
The pattern-only system provides strong precision at non-negligible recall, while model combinations recover additional recall.
Review-level inference: the approach offers a practical bridge between rule-based extraction and learned neural extraction under limited annotation.

value: Self-training introduces a precision–recall tradeoff: additional iterations improve recall but degrade precision.
The approach is sensitive to the quality of assumed negatives and requires a realistic, heavily negative class distribution.
The infrastructure is unusually resource-intensive, using a 20-core machine, 790 GB of memory, and a 1.2 TB PCI-E solid-state drive for the submissions.
The system's end-to-end evaluation does not cleanly distinguish entity-linking errors from relation-extraction errors.
Performance drops substantially from the slot-filling track to the KB track, indicating dependence on consistency and inference components.
Review-level inference: the method remains dependent on hand-written patterns and KBP-specific type/schema assumptions, limiting portability to new domains or relation inventories.
Review-level inference: reported gains are difficult to attribute uniquely to bootstrapping because the submission configurations combine multiple extractors and downstream components.
